games.title: Vector Breakout
games.tagline: The classic wall-breaker, rebuilt as light itself.
games.description:
Vector Breakout is the arcade wall-breaker stripped to its essence: one paddle, one beam, one wall of glowing bricks — and a score that climbs faster than your confidence.

Every brick you destroy feeds the beam a little more speed, so by the final rows the board is a reflex test rather than a puzzle. The board regenerates in twelve escalating layouts; survive all twelve and the wall rebuilds itself faster, forever.

Built to run in any browser with nothing installed, it's the flagship of the FreeGameplay arcade and the first game we ported when we rebuilt the site as a platform.
games.controls:
Move — A / D or the arrow keys (drag on touch)
Launch / Serve — Space
Pause — P
games.seoTitle: Vector Breakout — Free Browser Arcade Game
games.seoDescription: Play Vector Breakout free in your browser. The classic wall-breaker rebuilt for the modern web — 12 escalating layouts, no download.

games.title: Orbit Dodge
games.tagline: Thread the laser storm. Don't blink.
games.description:
Orbit Dodge drops you into a ring corridor of space and hands you a ship, a throttle and a lot of bad news in the form of red lasers.

The corridor scrolls continuously; bullets sweep, burst and spiral in patterns that repeat in twos and threes. Learn a pattern and it's free points — miss one and the run ends. Every run, the storm layers another pattern on top of the last, so depth always outlives you by exactly one idea.

It's the purest 'one more run' loop on the site, and the high-score ladder lives right beside the game.
games.controls:
Move — WASD or the arrow keys (drag on touch)
Pause — P
games.seoTitle: Orbit Dodge — Free Browser Space Dodger
games.seoDescription: Dodge an endless storm of lasers in Orbit Dodge — a free browser arcade game with escalating bullet patterns and a local high-score ladder.

games.title: Neon Snake
games.tagline: A serpent of light on an infinite grid.
games.description:
Neon Snake is the 1998 browser classic with the dust wiped off: a serpent made of connected light, a grid that never ends, and an orb that makes you longer, faster and slightly more reckless.

The modern twist is the grid itself — it scrolls gently, so the walls you memorised in run three have moved by run four. Simple as a snake, deep as a pattern-recognition test.
games.seoDescription: Play Neon Snake free in your browser — the classic snake game reimagined as a serpent of light on a shifting grid.

games.title: Gravity Well
games.tagline: Slingshot a star around the dark.
games.description:
Gravity Well is a physics toy that becomes a game: your orb is a body with momentum, the black ring in the middle has opinions, and the rings of light you have to pass through are spaced exactly where they should not be.

One button. Tap to give the orb a push in the direction it's already moving — no steering, no braking, just timing. Every level is a different gravitational personality: some wells drag, some fling, some do both at once.

It plays like a jazz solo: the rules are small, the expressions are not.
games.controls:
Push — click / tap / Space (one input, timed)
Pause — P
games.seoTitle: Gravity Well — Free Browser Physics Puzzle
games.seoDescription: Slingshot a star around a singularity in Gravity Well — a one-button physics puzzle that plays like a jazz solo.

games.title: Caves of Qud
games.tagline: A 4,000-year-old dungeon with a culture war inside it.
games.description:
Caves of Qud is a free, open-source roguelike in which a thousand years of in-fiction civilisation have layered themselves into a single cavern — religions, economies, rivalries and all, all of them still running.

You don't play a hero. You play an organism: your body is a set of abilities, your memories are a set of stats, and every room you enter is a negotiation. Combat, diplomacy, and the slow accumulation of things that change who you are.

It's the deepest 'free game' on the site — measured in years rather than sessions. The full game is free on itch.io.
games.controls: Full keyboard roguelike controls — the game's in-engine reference covers everything. Allow at least an evening for the opening act.
games.seoTitle: Caves of Qud — Free Roguelike Review & Guide
games.seoDescription: Why Caves of Qud is the deepest free game on the web — a review and starting guide for the free open-source roguelike.

games.title: FTL: Light Years Away
games.tagline: Every ship is different. Every run is a story you tell afterwards.
games.description:
FTL is the fleet simulator that made 'roguelike' a business model: build a ship from random rooms, crew it with random people, and fight through a procedurally written war where your best weapons are repairs, morale and the occasional lucky shot.

The demo is free, in-browser-adjacent on itch.io, and is a genuinely complete experience — a full sector, a full enemy chain, and the exact tension the whole game runs on. If the demo gets you, the full game is worth every cent.
games.controls: Mouse-driven tactical play; time flows in real time and can be paused and slowed. The demo walks you through the basics on first launch.
games.seoTitle: FTL: Light Years Away — Free Demo & Review
games.seoDescription: Play the free FTL: Light Years Away demo and read why it's still the best fleet-roguelike ever shipped — review and tips.

games.title: Papers, Please
games.tagline: The most addictive stamp you will ever press.
games.description:
In Papers, Please you are a border inspector in a fictional cold-war state, and your job — checking documents, stamping APPROVED or DENIED, paying rent from the wage — is simultaneously the most tedious and most gripping job in gaming.

The rules are explicit. The catch is that the rules are not enough: the game constantly presents you with cases where following them hurts someone, and it never tells you what a good person does. You learn the moral weight of a stamp.

Free demo on itch.io; the full game is a short, devastating few hours.
games.controls: Mouse only: select documents, cross-reference, stamp. No keyboard required.
games.seoTitle: Papers, Please — Free Demo, Review & Walkthrough
games.seoDescription: Papers, Please review and free demo — the border-control game about the moral weight of a stamp.

games.title: Undertale
games.tagline: A role-playing game where you can be very, very good.
games.description:
Undertale inverts the contract of the RPG: every fight can be a conversation, every 'defeat' is a choice, and the game remembers exactly what kind of player you are — including the times you walked away mid-battle and came back.

It is also a masterclass in tone, shifting from the cozy pixel village to genuinely frightening territory in a single room transition, and doing it with 8-bit music and a cat face.

The full game is free to play on itch.io from the original developer. No spoilers, please — this is one of the few games where spoilers change the game itself.
games.controls: Keyboard: arrows to move, Z to interact/attack, X to menu. Battle timing uses the same keys.

games.seoDescription: Play Undertale free on itch.io — a no-spoiler starting guide to the RPG that remembers everything you do.

posts.title: The Comeback of the Browser Arcade
posts.excerpt: Browser games are having a second act — and this time the web is actually fast enough to mean it. What changed, and what it means for how we play.
posts.contentHtml:
For most of the last decade, "browser game" was a polite way of saying "low-budget game". Flash died, the golden age of portal sites faded into nostalgia, and anyone serious about games went to Steam, to consoles, to phone app stores.

That era is over. The web got fast. The games got better. And a quiet renaissance is happening in the places nobody expected: itch.io's embeddable catalog, HTML5 ports of classic arcade titles, and a new generation of developers who chose the browser not because it was easy, but because it is universal.

Why now?

Three things converged. First, browsers became game engines: WebGL, WebGPU, and low-latency input handling mean a browser tab can run experiences that in 2012 would have needed a dedicated machine. Second, distribution flattened: a game that lives at a URL has no install friction, no account wall, and no platform tax. Third — and this is the cultural part — the players grew up. The people who spent their childhoods on Miniclip and Kongregate are now the ones with disposable income and a soft spot for a paddle and a beam.

What's different this time

The old browser arcade was a content firehose: ten thousand games, most of them empty, all of them competing for the same banner ad slot. The new era is curated. A small set of genuinely well-made free games, each with an identity, a designer's intent, and a community. Quality is the business model, because quality is the only thing a URL can carry on its own.

The best distribution is no distribution. A game that lives at a URL is a game that lives everywhere.

That's the bet FreeGameplay is making: not the biggest arcade, but the best-kept one. Every game here is playable, every guide is written, and nothing is padded to fill a slot.

The browser arcade is back. It just stopped being a dump and started being a destination.
posts.author: elias
posts.seoTitle: The Comeback of the Browser Arcade — FreeGameplay
posts.seoDescription: Browser games are having a second act. Why the web finally got fast enough to matter, and what the curated arcade era means for players.

posts.title: Five Free Games You Can Play in Any Browser Right Now
posts.excerpt: No download, no account, no catch. Five free games you can be playing in the next thirty seconds — and what to do first in each.
posts.contentHtml:
The best game is the one that is already installed. Which is to say: the one that lives at a URL. Here are five free games you can play in any browser, in any order, right now.

1. Vector Breakout

The arcade wall-breaker rebuilt as light. Start slow — the first four layouts are a warm-up. Your first real test is layout five, where the beam stops forgiving your aim. Keep the paddle near the bottom third; the walls punish reach.

2. Orbit Dodge

Pure pattern recognition. The first thirty seconds teach you the basic sweep; after that, stop trying to dodge the lasers and start dodging the space where the lasers are about to be. That one mental shift doubles your average run.

3. Neon Snake

The classic with a modern catch: the grid moves. Don't plan five turns ahead — plan one, and keep your eyes on the edge of the grid, not the head of the snake.

4. Gravity Well

One button, infinite nuance. If your star keeps slingshooting too wide, push earlier, not harder. The well does the rest.

5. Caves of Qud

The deep end. If you want a game that gives you a year of content for free, this is it. Read the first act's codex entries — they're not lore padding, they're the rules.

All five are free, no account required. Go play something.

posts.title: Vector Breakout: How We Rebuilt a Classic for Modern Browsers
posts.excerpt: Behind the flagship: the design decisions, the physics tweaks and the one bug that kept the hi-score ladder honest.
posts.contentHtml:
When we set out to rebuild the wall-breaker, we made one rule: keep the 1976 skeleton, replace everything else. The paddle, the beam, the wall — those are the contract with the player. Everything around them was fair game.

The physics pass

Classic breakout has a secret: the beam's vertical speed is constant, and only the horizontal component changes on bounce. That's why the ball can get "stuck" in a slow diagonal for an eternity. We kept the constant vertical speed — it's what makes the game readable — but added a tiny horizontal drift after each paddle hit, capped so it never breaks the feel. The result: no stuck balls, no sense of the game "intervening".

Speed as a narrative

In our version, the board feeds the beam speed as you destroy bricks. This is deliberate: the game should end the way a set in a sport ends, with you losing to the thing you yourself built. The final layouts are fast enough that you're playing at the edge of what your monitor's response time allows.

The honest ladder

Every arcade game has a score ladder, and every score ladder has been faked at least once. Ours runs on a local record plus a server-side check on the top ten. When a player claims a score, the client sends the last N board states, not just the number. You can't fake a trajectory. This one detail is why we trust our own ladder — and why we can print it on the homepage without embarrassment.

A classic is a contract. You keep the terms; you just renegotiate the fine print.

The build took three months. The paddle code is 200 lines. We're proud of both facts.
posts.author: elias
posts.seoTitle: How We Rebuilt Vector Breakout for Modern Browsers
posts.seoDescription: The design decisions, physics tweaks and honest score-ladder engineering behind our flagship browser game.

posts.title: Why Free-to-Play Is the Future (And What 'Free' Should Mean)
posts.excerpt: The industry keeps arguing about paywalls. Here's a different argument: 'free' is the most powerful word in the gaming economy — if we keep it honest.
posts.contentHtml:
Every few years someone declares free-to-play dead, and every few years the market proves them wrong with a new record. The argument is over. The question now is what "free" is for.

Free as a doorway, not a trap

There are two philosophies of free. The first: free is the top of a funnel, and the game is a casino with a loading screen. The second: free is the product. The game you play for free is complete, the monetisation (if any) is cosmetic or time-based, and nobody's dark pattern is the business model. The first philosophy wins on revenue per user and loses on trust per decade. The second is harder to fund and easier to defend.

What the player actually pays

In an honest free model, the player pays in attention and in community. They pay by being the reason the next game gets made. That's not romanticising — it's just the actual economics of a curated arcade: the player's time, spent well, is the asset. Waste it and the model is over.

The bar we hold ourselves to

FreeGameplay's rule is simple: every game on this site must be playable to completion without paying a cent and without watching a single ad. No energy timers, no loot boxes, no "one more spin" economics. If a free game can't survive on the strength of the game, it isn't a free game — it's a lead generator, and it doesn't belong here.

Free is not a discount. It's a promise. The future of gaming belongs to whoever keeps it.
posts.author: elias
posts.seoTitle: Why Free-to-Play Is the Future — FreeGameplay
posts.seoDescription: What 'free' should mean in 2026: free as a doorway, not a trap, and the bar every game on this site has to meet.

posts.title: How to Improve Your Aim in Fast Arcade Games
posts.excerpt: You don't need better reflexes. You need better prediction. A practical drill routine for paddle games, dodgers and anything with a moving target.
posts.contentHtml:
The most common aim mistake is aiming at the thing. In any arcade game fast enough to matter, the target you're looking at is already where the target was. Improvement is almost never about reflexes — it's about stopping trying to catch up.

Lead the target

In Vector Breakout, the beam's angle after a paddle hit is a function of where it struck. That means the next hit location is knowable the instant the ball leaves the paddle. Train yourself to read the angle, not the ball: eyes up, paddle moving to where the angle points, not where the ball is.

The 10% rule

In dodgers like Orbit Dodge, you don't need the full gap — you need ten percent of it. Moving the minimum distance that keeps you safe preserves your options for the next pattern. Big swerves are how runs die: not to the laser you saw, but to the one you committed into.

Drill, don't grind

Twenty focused minutes beats two hours of autopilot. A useful routine: five minutes of one pattern until it's boring, then one new pattern, then mix. Boredom is the signal that the pattern is yours.

Reflexes get you to the ladder. Prediction is what keeps you on it.

Play one of the four browser games in the arcade for a week with a single drill in mind. Your score will do the arguing for you.

posts.title: From Blog to Platform: The FreeGameplay Rebuild
posts.excerpt: A few years ago this was a blog. Today it's a content platform on real infrastructure. Here's what changed, what we kept, and what the migration taught us.
posts.contentHtml:
FreeGameplay started as a blog in the classic sense: posts, labels, and a theme file. The games lived in embeds, the guides lived in posts, and the whole site was held together by a CMS built for people who write newsletters, not platforms that serve games.

What the blog was good at

Two things. Speed — publishing a post took seconds — and URLs. Every post had a permanent address that readers, and eventually search engines, came to rely on. Those two properties were non-negotiable in the rebuild: nothing that worked had the right to stop working.

What the rebuild changed

Content got a real model. Games are now their own thing — playable, searchable, filterable, linked from guides. Guides link to the games they cover. Posts link to both. The old flat structure of "a post with a label" became a connected graph, which is the difference between a blog and a platform.

The backend moved to the edge: a content API on Cloudflare Workers, a real database with full-text search, media on object storage, and a migration pipeline that could take the old site's export and land every post, page and label in the new structure without losing a URL. The old addresses don't die — they redirect, permanently, to the new home.

What it taught us

Migrations are not technical problems; they are trust problems. Every legacy URL that works is a promise kept. Every redirect that 404s is a reader who quietly leaves and never comes back. We built the redirect registry before the new homepage, on purpose.

The blog is gone. The platform is here. The games — that's the part you're already playing.

posts.seoTitle: From Blog to Platform: The FreeGameplay Rebuild

guides.title: Vector Breakout: Complete Beginner Guide
guides.excerpt: From your first paddle hit to layout twelve: everything you need to stop losing bricks to the bottom row.
guides.contentHtml:
Vector Breakout looks simple and plays deceptively hard. This guide is the shortest honest path from first contact to the final layouts.

The bottom-row problem

Ninety percent of early losses are the same: a ball that drifts toward the bottom corner with a shallow angle, and a paddle that can't reach it in time. The fix is not faster movement — it's angle control. Where the ball strikes the paddle determines its exit angle. Hit with the edge and the ball shoots out wide; hit with the centre and it goes straight up. Use the centre to rescue any ball that's drifting low.

Layout five is the wall

The first four layouts teach the basics; layout five is where the game stops being gentle. Two habits that carry you through:

  • Keep the paddle in the bottom third of the board — never chase the ball upward.
  • After every paddle hit, commit: decide the next save before the ball arrives, don't react to it.

Reading the speed

The board accelerates as you clear it. When you notice the ball crossing the board in under a second, shift from saving to positioning: get to the middle and let the geometry bring the ball to your centre stroke. Trying to control angles at maximum speed is how runs end at layout eight.

When to stop

After a loss at layout six or beyond, take a break. The game rewards calm; it punishes tilt more than any other arcade game on this site.
guides.author: freegameplay-team
guides.seoDescription: Angle control, layout five, and reading the speed: the shortest honest path through Vector Breakout.

guides.title: Orbit Dodge: Advanced Evasion Patterns
guides.excerpt: The three bullet patterns that kill experienced players, and the movement economy that beats all of them.
guides.contentHtml:
Once you're past the first hundred points, Orbit Dodge stops being a dodger and starts being a pattern-reader. Here are the patterns that separate a five-minute run from a twenty-minute one.

The sweep

Lasers that cross the corridor on a diagonal, evenly spaced. Beginners try to outrun the sweep; that's a fight you lose. The sweep has a head and a tail — the safe zone is always just behind the head of the line, moving parallel to it. Match its speed for two seconds and the sweep is no longer a threat.

The spiral

The spiral rotates, which means its gap rotates with it. The instinct is to chase the gap; the correct move is to sit at the corridor's radius and let the gap come to you. Movement is spent only when the spiral's gap passes your position and you need to step into the next one.

The burst

Three quick volleys from one point. The burst is beatable by not moving at all if you're outside its cone — which is why the real cost is the two moves you spent dodging the pattern before it. Movement economy: every dodge you didn't need is a dodge you can't afford later.

The storm isn't trying to kill you. It's trying to make you move. Stay boring.

The endgame

After four or five pattern layers, your only real skill is recovery: how fast you can find the calmest point in the corridor after a close call. Slow down, one input, then resume. Speed kills faster than bullets out there.
guides.author: elias
guides.seoDescription: Sweeps, spirals and bursts — the three bullet patterns that kill experienced players, and the movement economy that beats them.

guides.title: Neon Snake: High-Score Strategies
guides.excerpt: The shifting grid changes everything you thought you knew about snake. Here's how the top players actually play it.
guides.contentHtml:
If you learned snake on a static board, forget most of it. Neon Snake's grid drifts, and every classic trick needs a small correction.

Own the edge, not the centre

On a static board, the centre is safe. On a drifting grid, the centre is where the walls converge. Top players keep the snake within two cells of the leading edge — the edge the grid moves toward — where the effective play space is actually widest.

Length is a resource

Every orb you eat makes the snake harder to turn, but the board rewards length with score and with speed. The discipline is in the direction of growth: grow into open space, never into a corner. A corner with a long snake is a countdown, not a home.

The one-turn rule

Plan at most one turn ahead. On a moving grid, a five-turn plan is a fiction — the grid will have moved by turn three. One turn, commit, re-plan. It feels slower than it is.

When the grid accelerates

Late-game, the drift speeds up. Counterintuitively, this is your friend: the faster the grid moves, the more the effective space ahead of you opens. Lean into the drift instead of fighting it, and the board that looked dead is usually the widest it's been all run.

guides.seoDescription: The shifting grid changes everything you know about snake — how the top players actually play Neon Snake.

guides.title: Getting Started on FreeGameplay
guides.excerpt: How the site works, how the games are organised, and the five-minute tour if you're new here.
guides.contentHtml:
Welcome. This is the fastest honest tour of FreeGameplay.

How it's organised

Three things live here, and they link to each other:

  • Games — the arcade. Every game is playable, free, and no-account. The four browser games run right on the page; the external ones open on itch.io in a new tab.
  • Guides — strategy writing for specific games. Each guide is linked from the game it covers, and vice versa.
  • The blog — longer pieces on the browser arcade, free-to-play, and the site itself.

Five-minute tour

One: open Vector Breakout and play one full layout. Two: read the two-paragraph beginner guide for it. Three: try Orbit Dodge for three minutes. Four: read the advanced patterns guide and notice how much more the storm makes sense. Five: come back tomorrow. That's the whole product loop — play, read, understand, return.

House rules

No paywalls, no energy timers, no ad walls between you and the game. High scores are local and honest — the ladders run on verified trajectories, not on whatever number a client sends up. If you find a broken link, a missing image, or a guide that doesn't make sense, the contact page actually goes somewhere.

That's it. The games are why you're here; go play something.

pages.title: About FreeGameplay
pages.contentHtml:
FreeGameplay is a hand-curated arcade of free browser games with deep guides, reviews and writing around them. No downloads, no paywalls, no fluff.

The standard

Every game on this site must be playable to completion without paying a cent. Every guide must be written by someone who played the game. Every legacy URL from the old site must still work. Those three rules are the whole editorial policy.

The stack

Under the surface: a content API on Cloudflare Workers, a Postgres-grade content model in a D1 database with full-text search, media on R2 object storage, and a Next.js frontend built to load fast on a phone at a train station. The boring parts are done properly on purpose.

The origin

This started as a blog about the browser arcade in the mid-2020s and became a platform when the writing kept pointing at the games. The rebuild that got us here — from blog to platform, without losing a single old URL — is documented on the blog.

pages.title: Contact
pages.contentHtml:
Found a broken link? A guide that doesn't make sense? A free game you think deserves a slot in the arcade? Send it — the form below goes to a real inbox, and everything gets read.

For anything about rights, takedowns or partnerships, include the word partnership or takedown in the subject so it routes correctly.

pages.title: Privacy Policy
pages.contentHtml:
Short version: we run a content and games site. We collect as little as possible, we don't sell data, and we don't run ad trackers.

What we store

  • Contact messages — if you use the contact form, we store your name, email and message so we can answer. Nothing else is attached to it.
  • High scores — arcade high scores are stored locally in your browser. The verified ladder on the homepage stores scores only, not identities.
  • Analytics — privacy-conscious, aggregate analytics only. No cross-site tracking, no fingerprinting, no ad cookies.

What we don't do

  • No third-party ad networks.
  • No selling or sharing personal data.
  • No dark patterns, no consent walls for playing.

Your data

If you sent us a message and want it deleted, contact us and we'll delete it. If you want your local high score gone, clear your browser storage for this site. That's the whole inventory.

Questions about this policy go to the contact page. We answer like the rest of the site: properly, and eventually.
